tip: 'Hacerse' in impersonal expressions: 'se me hace tarde' = it's getting late for me. The 'me' shows who it's happening to.
Why the -s on 'cumpleaños'? It's 'cumple' + 'años' – 'completes years'. One birthday, always spelled plural: 'hoy es mi cumpleaños'.
'Escribo' covers both 'I write' and 'I'm writing'. Spanish rarely needs an -ing form – the simple present does double duty.
Weather uses 'hacer' in Spanish: 'hace calor' (it's hot), 'hace frío' (it's cold), 'hace sol' (it's sunny), 'hace viento' (it's windy).
'Para llevar' = for taking away. Standard phrase for takeout food.
Very sunny? Spanish says much sun: 'hace mucho sol'. Since 'sol' is a noun, 'muy' won't fit – it pairs with adjectives, 'mucho' with nouns.
No -ly needed: 'rápido' works as its own adverb in 'como demasiado rápido'. Many everyday adjectives moonlight as adverbs unchanged.
Order water abroad and you'll be asked: '¿con o sin gas?'. Here 'sin gas' = still, 'con gas' = sparkling – literally without/with gas.
Estar marks a current condition: 'la sopa está fría' means cold right now. It also answers '¿cómo estás?' – someone's mood, health, or state.
'Ilusión' is not an illusion here – it's happy anticipation, so 'me hace ilusión verte' = I'm thrilled to see you. A famously positive false friend.
'Es ingeniero' – no 'un'. After 'ser', a profession works like a label, so Spanish drops the article. It comes back when you add an adjective: 'es un ingeniero brillante'.
'Para' marks a deadline (by/for): in 'necesito esto para el lunes', 'para' sets Monday as the time limit.
'Al centro' shows a mandatory contraction: 'a' + 'el' fuse into 'al'. The other one is 'del' ('de' + 'el').
'Grande' after the noun means big in size: 'familia grande'. Slide it in front and it shrinks to 'gran' – 'una gran familia' – and the meaning shifts to 'great'.
You don't 'be' right in Spanish – you have it: 'tienes razón' is literally 'you have reason'. Same trick as 'tener hambre' (hunger) and 'tener sueño' (sleepiness).
'Para' here aims at a destination: 'vamos para el aeropuerto' = heading toward it. Swap in 'por' and you'd be passing by way of the airport – route, not goal.
Estar for appearance now: 'estás muy guapa hoy'. How someone looks right now, vs. 'ser' for general beauty.
'Puede' could mean 'he/she can' or 'you (formal) can'. 'puedes' is unambiguous – always the informal you. Spanish reuses the third-person form for formal you.
'Carro' = car in Latin America; in Spain a 'carro' is a cart – they say 'coche'. Same rental, different word depending where you land.
'Tener' + noun for physical states: 'tener sed' (be thirsty), 'tener hambre' (be hungry).
'Que' + subjunctive expresses wishes: 'que descanses' = may you rest / rest well. The subjunctive conveys hope or desire.
'De ... a ...' marks a range: 'de lunes a viernes' = from Monday to Friday.
English stacks nouns: plug adapter. Spanish reverses with 'de': 'adaptador de enchufes' – adapter of plugs. The main noun comes first.
'Ve' is the irregular command of 'ir'; add 'te' (from 'irse', to take yourself off) and you get 'vete' – a brisk 'off you go'.
'En casa', no article, means at home in general. Add the article and 'en la casa' points at the physical building – with it, the place; without it, the concept.
No 'does' needed: Spanish negates with a bare 'no' before the verb, as in 'no tiene wifi' = it doesn't have wifi. One little word does it all.
'Ella' is optional here – 'quiere' already shows who. Native speakers drop subject pronouns unless contrasting (I, not him).
'Desde hace años' is literally 'since it makes years'. Spanish counts elapsed time with 'hace', so the plain present 'conozco' does the job of English's 'I have known'.
'Es bueno' rates the coffee's overall quality; 'está bueno' would praise this particular cup – tasty right now. 'ser' gives the general judgment, 'estar' the current instance.
Sun and heat use 'hace', but rain and snow are full verbs: 'está nevando' = it's snowing (from 'nevar'). 'nieva', 'llueve' – no 'hace' in sight.
